For both yr1:T and Sr1:T, we carry out pair-wise comparisons across all frames, resulting in the comparison matrices Mr and f Mr respectively, as shown in Figure 3. Specifically, each entry in the matrix Mr is given by: Mrpq = ↑, yrq > yrp; ↓, yrq < yrp; =, yrq = yrp.

decision_rationale: Full text shows a valid in-scope preference signal: conversion of numeric interval ratings into ordinal/relative comparisons (ROL) and explicit use of pairwise comparison matrices. The work is applied to speech datasets (MSP-Podcast/Conversation) and is original research with an HMM trained via Baum-Welch (i.e., a learning component), so no exclusion criteria apply. Per the decision policy, all inclusion criteria are satisfied and no exclusion is triggered; recommend include (stage_score=5).
short_summary: The paper proposes and trains an HMM-based method to convert time-continuous interval emotion ratings into time-continuous ordinal labels (including relative comparisons), evaluates on speech corpora, and is primary research rather than a survey; it meets inclusion criteria and is not evaluation-only.
disagreement_resolution: Junior ledgers conflicted on whether the paper presents an in-scope preference-learning path (I1) and whether preferences are evaluation-only (E1). I reviewed the full text: it explicitly describes converting interval (numeric) ratings into ROL-style comparative signals (including pairwise framewise comparisons and construction of comparison matrices Mr and fMr) and also trains HMMs (Baum-Welch) to produce AOL sequences. Therefore I resolved I1 in favor of junior_nano (YES) because conversion of numeric ratings into ordinal/relative comparisons meets the criterion. I resolved E1 in favor of junior_nano (NO) because the paper contains an explicit model-training step (HMM parameter estimation) rather than using preferences solely for post-hoc evaluation. Overall I followed the junior_nano judgment and issue a final include.
